trace: The framework here asks for post-earnings technicals plus a GTC read-through on NVDA, so I need to decide first whether the setup is still a buy or whether the parabolic move has exhausted itself. Price has settled above the 20-day EMA near 1150 and RSI has bled off from 85 down to 62, which to me reads as digestion rather than distribution, and the high-volume node at 1100 gives me a real shelf to lean on rather than an arbitrary round number. The honest tension is the MACD histogram flattening even while the lines stay crossed bullish. I can tell that two ways, and I should say so: healthy consolidation is my read, but smart-money distribution at a top deserves maybe 30% weight. On fundamentals the numbers do a lot of work for me. Forward P/E around 45x looks scary in isolation, but against roughly 85% EPS growth, Data Center at about 85% of revenue growing 110%, ROE of 91% and ROCE of 61%, the multiple is not the binding constraint. GTC mattered less for hardware than for lock-in, the NIM software layer and robotics widening the TAM. For scenarios I want a heavy base case, 65% at 1450 using 40x on FY2026 EPS of 36.25, 25% bull at 1800 on sovereign AI and software re-rating, and 10% bear at 900 if hyperscalers digest. Probability-weighting gives 1482.50, above spot near 1200, so accumulate on dips with adds above 1260 and a re-evaluation on a weekly close under the 50-day EMA at 1050. My macro confidence should stay low, around 55%, because the capex cycle duration is genuinely unknowable, and recency bias is the bias to flag. If wrong, the tells are HBM and TSMC order cuts, cautious hyperscaler capex language, and Blackwell ASP pressure.

Micron over nine months is really a question about where we are in the memory cycle, and I want to be honest that this is the hardest part to call. The structural piece I believe in is HBM: AI server demand is real, HBM3E should ramp toward the 20-25% share we have modeled, and that supports my 80% confidence on the fundamental thesis even while I only give 70% to the probability weights and 65% to the base-case target. For the base case at 60% I assume an orderly recovery, DRAM and NAND spot up 15-20% across three quarters, DRAM contributing 5-7% per quarter and NAND 4-6%, gross margin climbing from roughly 30% toward 45-50%. Eighteen times forward is mid-cycle, not heroic, and gets me to 155 within eight to ten months. The bull case at 25% is a genuine super-cycle: pull-forward ordering, double-ordering visible in channel checks, DRAM spot up 40-50%, multiple expanding to 25x for a 210 target, with roughly 12 dollars of fair value for every 10% surprise in the spot index. The bear leans on macro, trade escalation, higher-for-longer rates where 100bps historically shaves 3-4% off semi sales growth within two quarters, plus HBM yield stumbles. What nags at me is that the price may already embed the base case and part of the bull, and the insider selling reads as a contrarian tell that management sees fair value. Recency bias is the trap, since the commodity nature of the business has not been repealed by AI. So my trigger is a break of the 50-day EMA at 130, after which I check weekly DRAMeXchange spot, competitor inventory builds at Samsung and SK Hynix, and shrinking GPU lead times.

Lululemon is a brand-quality story colliding with a normalizing consumer, and the whole judgment is whether the premium multiple survives that. I keep coming back to margins as the real fulcrum rather than revenue. My base case, which I want at 60%, assumes 13-15% revenue growth and 15-18% EPS growth with gross margin slipping 50bps to 58.0% as promotions normalize, and a 28x forward multiple in line with the five-year average, which gives 385. Technically the 200-day SMA around 340 and the high-volume node at 350 form the zone I would actually buy into, with RSI drifting 45-60 rather than stretched. The bull case at 25% and 450 requires China revenue growth above 50% plus footwear and men's contributing more than five points of growth while Alo and Vuori fail to take share. That last condition is the one I trust least, so I will not weight it higher. The bear at 15% and 290 is a promotional cascade plus a North American consumer pullback. I should name my own bias here, which is brand loyalty bias, assuming past resilience automatically extends. The counterargument worth stating is that TAM saturation plus a no-room-for-error valuation means recent weakness is de-rating, not a dip. The stress test helps me stay constructive: cutting the five-year revenue CAGR 300bps and terminal gross margin 200bps still leaves fair value near 320, so there is a cushion. That drives the plan: accumulate, half position at 340-350, second half on reclaiming the 50-day EMA near 375, target 385, stop on a weekly close below 315. If it breaks 320, I check sequential gross margin, inventory growth outrunning sales by more than 500bps, and web traffic and app downloads.

This Eli Lilly setup is a binary event trade dressed up as a fundamental analysis, and I need the structure to reflect that. Donanemab's TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 4 readout dominates near-term price action, so the honest framing is scenario weights on trial outcomes plus a valuation bridge from peak sales. My base case, 60%, is positive but messy: the primary endpoint is met with 25-35% slowing on iADRS, but ARIA-E above 20% or weak APOE4 non-carrier efficacy narrows the label. That supports 6-8 billion in peak sales, roughly 45 dollars per share on my sum-of-the-parts, with the core diabetes and oncology franchise compounding 12%, and I get 790 at 45x forward after a gap into the 780-800 zone. The bull at 25% is unambiguous, above 40% slowing with ARIA-E under 15%, peak sales revised to 12-15 billion, 90 to 110 dollars per share, a breakaway gap above 820 and a run at 900 with RSI over 80. The bear takes the stock back to 570 on a 35x peer multiple, a 15-20% single-session drop testing 550-580. Because the outcome is binary, holding a full position into the print is not defensible; a call spread caps risk, and trimming 25-30% is the pragmatic hedge. My confidence should be honest too: framework 75%, probability assignment only 60%, valuation transmission 70%. The bias I am most exposed to is availability, anchoring on Leqembi's recent success when Alzheimer's historically fails over 99% of the time. Peak sales are the fragile input, since a five point shift in penetration moves the bull case more than 30 dollars a share. And if the base case prints but the stock falls, I look at risk-off tape or competitor pipeline read-through.

Block is the kind of name where the narrative has been promised for years and only partly delivered, so I want a wide, neutral-leaning framework rather than a call. The base case, 60% weight, is that a sluggish macro keeps Cash App gross profit growing 15-18% and Square seller GPV 8-10%, with adjusted EBITDA margin up 150-200bps as the Rule of 40 discipline bites. That is a profitability story, not a growth story, so I apply 9x EV/gross profit, slightly under the three-year average, and land on 80. The chart agrees with the range framing: support near 50, the 200-day SMA around 75 as the ceiling, MACD histogram hugging zero and RSI stuck 45-55, which is exactly what a stock with no thesis resolution looks like. The bull at 25% needs a soft landing plus real cross-sell evidence, two quarters of gross profit growth above 20% and Cash App Pay landing inside the Square merchant base, which would justify 12x and 115. The bear takes it back under 50 toward 45. Overall confidence sits around 65% because the competitive intensity is high and macro is doing a lot of the work. My blind spot is confirmation bias on management execution; shifting a growth culture toward cost discipline is harder than a slide deck suggests, and the Cash App and Square synergy is a story with modest historical proof. The alternative reading I should give air to is that weakness signals Cash App has peaked in the US with marketing spend hitting diminishing returns. So: sell cash-secured puts near 50, buy on a weekly close above 75 with a stop at 70, and watch MAU deceleration and two quarters of Square transaction margin contraction as the falsifiers.

Three to six months is a short enough window on NVDA that I should lean on technical structure and near-term catalysts rather than trying to relitigate the long-run AI thesis. The setup I see is a stock that has already run hard and now needs to digest: I expect consolidation between the 850 shelf, which was prior resistance, and the round 1000 level, with RSI cooling out of overbought into a 55-65 band, the 50-day EMA acting as dynamic support, and a MACD histogram that is shrinking while staying above the signal. That combination argues for patience rather than chasing. My base case at 55% assumes Data Center demand stays strong but decelerates, revenue growth around 80% versus the prior 100%-plus, gross margin near 75%, ROE still above 90%, with China headwinds already discounted. Applying 38x forward, a mild compression, gives me 1050. The bull at 30% needs Blackwell pre-orders, a sovereign deal, or hyperscaler capex upgrades to push the multiple to 45x and the price to 1300, and I would want confirmation from a break above 1020 with ADX over 40 and OBV at new highs. The bear at 15% is the inventory digestion scenario, which I actually think is the most plausible way the bull thesis breaks, and it puts the stock back at the 200-day SMA around 750. Netting that out, the risk-reward for new capital at current levels is not compelling, so hold with a cautious-buy tilt: add on dips toward the 50-day near 900, trim above 1050, reduce below 850, exit under 750. Macro confidence stays 55% because none of this survives a capex revision. Earliest warnings are sequential Data Center deceleration, rising supplier days of inventory at TSM, and cloud capex cuts.

Stretching NVDA out to twelve months changes what matters: the technical picture becomes less decisive and valuation sustainability becomes the whole argument, which is why I rate technicals 85% but fundamentals only 65% and competitive factors 60%. My base case at 55% is deceleration without disruption. Revenue growth falls to 80-100% from north of 200%, gross margin holds 75-77% on H100 and H200 pricing power, and the forward multiple compresses from roughly 75x to 40-45x. Custom silicon like Google's TPU and Amazon's Trainium supplements rather than displaces, which is the key distinction. At 45x on FY2026 EPS I get 1150, with the volume profile support at 850-900 and RSI settling into 50-60 as the parabolic move unwinds. The bull at 30% requires Blackwell benchmarks beating by more than 30%, over 20 billion in sovereign deals, and AMD and Intel continuing to miss, which would justify 55x and 1500. The bear at 15% is an AI air pocket plus custom-chip erosion dragging gross margin under 70%, a 200-day break with a head-and-shoulders top and negative OBV, and 30x on cut estimates for 750. The analogy I cannot ignore is Cisco in 2000, where the technology was genuinely real and the multiple still reset, and I should admit my framework may underweight that. The fair counter is that the market may simply be pricing a paradigm leader correctly. Given the spread, the honest call is hold rather than buy, use covered calls for income, add near the 50-day around 900, add on a breakout above 1000 with 150% volume, and cut half on three consecutive closes under the 200-day. Underperformance versus SOXX plus MI300X traction is my early competitive warning.

Lululemon at 310 is a very different problem than it was at 515, and I need to resist both the falling-knife instinct and the value trap instinct. The tape is clearly broken: a decline of more than 35%, price under the 20, 50 and 200-day EMAs, only a shelf near the 300 psychological level from mid-2023 holding it up. RSI at 35.8 is climbing off oversold but has not reclaimed 40, let alone 50. The MACD is below both signal and zero with the histogram ticking up, so momentum is decelerating rather than reversing, and the 20-day SMA near 318 remains unreclaimed. Capitulation volume on the late-May gap down followed by average volume tells me neither side has conviction. That is a 65% confidence read at best. Fundamentally the story is moderation, not deterioration: forward P/E of about 24x is a real contraction from the historic 35-40x premium, price to sales 4.5x, PEG about 1.8, gross margin still best-in-class near 57%, operating margin 20%, ROE around 30%, balance sheet clean. But growth is guided down to roughly 11% from 19% with Americas softness, and China carrying the load. That combination is not cheap enough to buy aggressively nor broken enough to short. So neutral is the defensible call: tactical entries in 295-305 for the aggressive, prudent buyers waiting for a weekly close above the 50-day near 345 with a MACD crossover, stop on a weekly close under 290, and a 265 bear target if the multiple compresses to 20x on sub-55% margins. The alternative I must respect is that this is a bear flag, not a base. If 290 breaks, I check Americas store traffic, website discounting versus peers, and China GDP revisions.

Palantir over three to six months is a question about whether AIP adoption is linear or about to inflect, and I genuinely cannot resolve that with the data available, which is why my commercial revenue model confidence is only 60% against 80% for government. The base case at 60% is the boring one: US commercial customer count keeps growing 40-50% QoQ, bootcamps convert into roughly one million dollar deals over six months, government grows about 15% with one or two sub-100 million awards and no new billion-dollar prize, and adjusted operating margin holds 33-35% while SBC keeps weighing on GAAP. At 22x forward EV/Sales, in line with the recent average for around 30% growth, I land at 26. Technically that means continued range trade between the 200-day near 20 and prior resistance at 27.50, with a flat MACD and RSI at 45-60. The bull at 25% needs a genuine S-curve, a Fortune 50 nine-figure signing or a pulled-forward C-JADC2 award, expanding the multiple to 30x and the price to 38 on 40-45% growth. The bear is where I have to be self-critical: the same flat chart I call consolidation could be distribution, insiders sell persistently, and SBC masks the absence of real economic profit. Overall confidence 65%, with recency bias the named risk after two strong quarters. The stress test comforts me a little, since zeroing government growth still leaves a 22 base target, implying the commercial story is the floor. My falsifiers are clear: commercial customer growth under 25% QoQ, billings lagging revenue, accelerating Form 4 sales, and if 20 breaks without a macro cause I go to alternative data on bootcamp and enterprise activity.

With Lilly the analysis has to be built around two launches happening at once, Zepbound and donanemab, and the honest risk is that concentration rather than any single drug failing. I am comfortable at 85% on the underlying franchise because Verzenio and Jardiance keep compounding, but only 70% on the scenario weights and 65% on the target, because launch curves are wide. The base case, 60%, has Zepbound taking 35-40% of the branded obesity market by end of 2025 against Wegovy, donanemab approved but slow off the line on reimbursement and ARIA monitoring, revenue growing 22-25%, Zepbound peak sales around 25 billion, donanemab at 1.5 billion in 2025, and operating margin up 150bps on mix. At 55x forward, a touch above the five-year average, that supports 950, with the stock basing between the 50-day EMA and the prior high, RSI easing to 55-60 and volume profile support at 750. The bull at 25% is capacity-constrained share above 50%, a favorable CMS coverage decision, and a pipeline surprise. Against a current price near 850, that risk-reward supports a partial position now with tiered adds above 900 on volume and a hard stop under 740. Where I need discipline is bias: recency bias from a stellar run, and the possibility the multiple is a safety premium rather than a growth premium, which would bleed away in a risk-on rotation into higher beta. If the thesis is failing, the tells are sequential deceleration in IQVIA weekly Zepbound scripts, gross margin failing to expand with the new mix, and physician commentary about the practical burden of administering donanemab.

Working NVDA on a split-adjusted basis here, with the 50-day EMA near 118 and the 200-day around 91, the question is whether current price already discounts the base case. I think it largely does, which points toward accumulating weakness rather than buying strength. The base case gets 65% because roughly 90% share in AI data center GPUs is not a share that erodes in two quarters, revenue should hold 60-70% growth for the next two prints, gross margin 75-77%, and a 40x forward multiple against a PEG near 1.2 is not the excess people assume. At 42x on FY2025 consensus I get 145. Technically the trend is intact: price above the 50-day EMA that has held for eighteen months, ADX above 40, OBV making new highs, which is institutional accumulation rather than distribution. The bull at 25% needs Blackwell to be a genuine super cycle plus 15-20 billion of sovereign demand and software above 10% of revenue, taking the multiple to 50x and the price to 170, with roughly 8 dollars of target for each 500bps of surprise growth. The bear I keep small at 10%, tighter export controls or custom silicon, de-rating to 30x and 105. That gives a probability-weighted 148.25, modestly above spot, so accumulate in 115-120 with a weekly close below the 200-day at 91 as the invalidation and trimming a quarter at 170. My honest weaknesses are confirmation bias given how one-sided the narrative is, and possibly underrating semiconductor cyclicality. Insider selling could be read as management seeing a peak. Below the 50-day I would check cloud capex channel checks, MI300X lead times, and new Commerce Department export language.

Enphase at 125.50 is fundamentally a rates trade wearing a technology costume, and I need the framework to say that plainly. My base case, 55%, has the Fed funds rate parked at 5.00-5.25%, financing costs high but not deteriorating further, residential demand recovering slowly, Europe carrying some of the load, revenue up only 2-4% sequentially and gross margin stabilizing at 43-44%. At 35x forward EV/EBITDA, the three-year median, that is 135, consistent with the stock chopping in the 110-140 range above the 200-day with RSI near 50. The bull at 25% requires an actual dovish pivot: two or more cuts priced by year-end, long yields falling, IQ9 adoption running ahead, a 10% revenue beat and raised guidance. I model each 50bps decline in the ten-year adding about 3% to US installation growth and 4-5% to revenue, and a re-rate to 45x gets 180. The bear at 20% is higher-for-longer plus NEM 3.0 and margin erosion, taking it to 90 with support at 100. Weighting those gives 138.25, only modestly above spot, and the downside in the bear case is roughly 44%, so the honest call is speculative hold with position size held to 1-2% rather than any conviction buy. Overall confidence 60% is right given how much sits outside management's control. My bias risk is anchoring to the old highs above 300, which makes 125 feel cheap when the market may have structurally changed. The stability could equally be a bear flag, maybe 30% odds. Below 110 I check distributor sell-through, and a ten-year above 4.5% kills the base case.

This second pass at Enphase frames the valuation off sales rather than EBITDA, so I want the drivers stated in demand and inventory terms. Base case, 60%: the ten-year stabilizes at 4.0-4.5%, US residential contracts about 5% in 2024 before returning to 5-10% growth in 2025, European revenue grows around 10% sequentially as 2023 inventory clears, IQ8 keeps leadership and battery attach holds near 20%. Applying 6.5x forward EV/Sales, slightly under the five-year average to reflect normalization, I get 135 over nine to twelve months, confirmed or denied by the next two prints. The bull at 25% needs 100-150bps of cuts, with each 50bps adding 3-4% to US demand, plus Brazil, India and Australia contributing an extra 150 million a quarter by Q4 2025 and IQ9 expanding the TAM, which supports 9.0x and 190. The bear at 15% turns on policy risk around IRA credits and net metering in Texas and Florida, confirmed by two straight quarters of negative revenue growth and gross margin under 40%, targeting 75. I set macro and policy confidence at only 55% because the rate path is the dominant variable and my stabilization assumption is the single point of failure. The interpretation that worries me most is that channel inventory reflects saturation in mature markets like California rather than a cycle, which would break both the base and bull. The commoditization argument on premium pricing also deserves weight if IQ9 underwhelms. Stress testing rates at 5%-plus for eighteen months pushes the stock toward 50-60. Below 90 I check gross margin under 42%, a third quarter of falling sell-through, and EU growth under 5% sequentially.

LVMH is really a proxy on the Chinese consumer, so I want to be explicit about how much of the valuation rests on a recovery I cannot yet see. Base case at 60% assumes uneven but real improvement in Chinese confidence with targeted stimulus, resilient US and European demand, organic revenue growth of 8% and EPS growth of 10%, with Fashion and Leather Goods, the profit engine, up 9% and ROIC holding near 18%. A DCF at 7.5% WACC and 3% terminal growth cross-checked against 24x forward gives me 820 euros, with the 200-day at 745 as durable support, RSI parked 45-55 and a MACD that is trying to cross but lacks thrust, exactly what a gradual recovery looks like. The bull at 25% and 950 requires a bazooka stimulus; I size the transmission as a one trillion RMB consumer package lifting luxury spending 8-10%, which given China at 25-30% of sales is a 4-5% revenue uplift, plus returning tourists and a weaker euro. The bear at 15% and 610 on 18x is a deepening property crisis. Balanced like that, hold with accumulation on weakness is the only defensible stance. My exposed assumption is brand elasticity in the second-tier portfolio, Tiffany and the watch houses, which are far more cyclical than Louis Vuitton or Dior, and I should flag status quo bias, the assumption LVMH is downturn-proof, with the 2022-2023 US normalization as the counterexample. The consolidation could be distribution given weak up-day volume. Warning signs are the Hang Seng under 16,000, Fashion and Leather organic growth under 5% for two quarters, and VIX above 25. The most likely failure is a slow bleed, roughly 40% within the base case, worth minus 15%.

Snowflake sits at the intersection of a real AI tailwind and a real competitive threat, and my confidence should reflect that: 65% overall, 75% on fundamentals, only 55% on the probability weights because macro moves the multiple more than execution does. Base case, 60%: product revenue growth settles at 28-32%, non-GAAP product margin holds 75-76%, net revenue retention recovers modestly to about 135%, and competition from Databricks, AWS and Google stays intense but rational without a price war. Fifteen times forward EV/Sales, a little under the three-year average to reflect maturing growth, gives 185 over six to nine months, with the stock basing near 140 and eventually reclaiming the 200-day that currently caps it, RSI 45-65. The bull at 25% needs Cortex and Snowpark Container Services to convert into consumption, two quarters of growth reaccelerating past 40%, NRR back above 145%, and a volume-confirmed break of 200, which supports a 20x re-rate and 240, helped by a dovish Fed compressing the discount rate on long-duration cash flows. The bear at 15% is the one I might be underweighting: the deeper question is whether a closed, consumption-priced platform holds up in an open-source AI world, and if Databricks momentum is stronger than public data shows, my weights are wrong. With beta around 1.5 I want a smaller position, options to define risk into earnings, a stop near 132, and a full rethink if NRR prints below 130%. Anchoring to old highs is the bias to guard. If wrong bearishly, I check erosion in million-dollar customers; if wrong cautiously, a surge in RPO is the tell.

Micron on a three to six month view is a timing problem: I am fairly convinced the cycle has bottomed, roughly 85% confident on direction, but only about 60% on timing and magnitude, which nets to 70% overall. The base case at 55% is an orderly recovery, DRAM and NAND prices up 5-10% per quarter as channel inventory normalizes, HBM for AI servers providing a tailwind while smartphones and PCs stay lukewarm. Revenue growth accelerates to 20-25%, gross margin climbs from roughly 20% toward 30-35%, ROCE turns up off the trough, and at 4.5x forward price to sales, typical for early-to-mid recovery, I get 150. The chart fits: consolidation above the 50-day EMA near 128, RSI in a constructive 55-65, and a volume shelf at 120. The bull at 30% is a genuine AI supercycle with HBM3e and HBM4 demand from NVIDIA and AMD overshooting, competitor yield problems handing Micron pricing power, revenue growth above 50% and gross margin past 45%, confirmed technically by clearing 155 on volume and riding the upper Bollinger Band, giving 175. The bear at 15% brings back the glut, single-digit margins, a potential death cross and falling OBV, and 110 at 3.0x sales. Netting that, cautiously optimistic is the right posture rather than table-pounding, and my main self-criticism is over-weighting AI when HBM is still small next to conventional DRAM and NAND, with the P/S already at the high end of its range. Warning signs are DRAM spot flattening for two weeks, cloud capex guidance, and rising inventory days. Below 120 I check Samsung's semiconductor results, ISM manufacturing, and a VIX spike.

Adobe is the cleanest test I have of whether generative AI is a moat or a solvent, and I do not think the market has settled it, which is why I land on a scenario-dependent hold rather than a directional call. Base case at 55%: Firefly gets embedded across Creative Cloud and Experience Cloud, supports modest price increases and better retention, Digital Media grows 11-13% with a 3-5% ARR uplift from Firefly, ROE stays near 40% and net margin settles at 28-29% after the AI investment build. Thirty times forward, slightly under the five-year average to acknowledge Canva and the AI-native entrants, gives 580. That squares with the tape, range-bound between the 50-week SMA at 510 and recent highs near 630, MACD histogram at zero, RSI 45-60. The bull at 30% needs enterprise Firefly API adoption and ARR accelerating past 15%, justifying 38x and 720 with short-term FCF growth revised to 20%, triggered by a break above the 699 all-time high. The part I am least comfortable defending is the 15% bear weight; the pace of generative AI disruption is unprecedented and I am leaning on Adobe's historical adaptability, which is close to brand loyalty bias. The sideways action could be a distribution top instead of consolidation, maybe 35% likely, and I would want rising down-day volume and negative OBV divergence as evidence. Stress testing, the base holds at 9% Digital Media growth but fails on a 300bps margin contraction from pricing pressure. So: hold, write covered calls above 650, add above 640 on 150% volume, halve below the 200-day and exit under 500. If a breakout fails, check Firefly API call volumes, single-app churn in the 10-Q, and Canva Pro and Midjourney traffic.

Deere is a cyclical business trying to argue it is becoming a subscription business, and the whole twelve-month thesis is whether precision ag can smooth the downcycle in large equipment. Base case at 60%: a soft landing, corn and soybean prices stabilizing, farmer balance sheets normalizing but healthy, Production and Precision Ag revenue down a modest 5-8% while Small Ag and Turf is flat, offset by 25% growth in precision ag recurring revenue lifting gross margin 50bps. That gets me EPS near 28.00, and at 14.6x forward, the five-year average, a 410 target, with the stock ranging between 360 at the 200-week SMA and 440, MACD flat and RSI 45-55. The bull at 20% and 495 needs a Black Sea supply shock rallying grains plus 75-100bps of Fed cuts lowering farmer financing costs and more than 35% precision ag growth. The bear at 20% and 320 is a hard landing where a 15% drop in corn and soy cuts net farm income more than 20% and large equipment sales fall 15-20%, EPS to 22.50 at a trough 14.2x, with Deere Capital's own funding costs squeezing net interest margin. What I need to flag as my blind spot is the assumption that precision ag revenue is anti-cyclical; in a severe downturn farmers cut subscriptions too, and that assumption carries both the base and bull. Confidence is 75% on the base but only 50% on the bull because tail events are hard to weight. Flat to declining OBV supports reading the consolidation as distribution near a cycle top. Below 360 I check used large tractor dealer inventories, precision ag take rates on new equipment, and Deere Capital 30-day delinquencies.

For NVDA over twelve months the framework asks me to hold three things at once: demand, Taiwan, and competition, and they do not carry equal confidence. I am 85% confident on demand, 70% on the competitive picture, but only 60% on geopolitical stability, which is where the real tail sits. Base case at 60%: H100, H200 and Blackwell demand stays robust, TSMC CoWoS packaging eases but still gates supply, which conveniently preserves pricing power, AMD's MI300X and in-house silicon at Google and Amazon take minor share, and China settles at a lower baseline post-controls. Data Center grows about 150% for two more quarters before moderating, ROE stays above 60%, forward P/E near 35x against 80% EPS growth. At 40x on projected EPS of 27.50 I get 1100, with about 50 dollars of target for every 5% change in Data Center growth. The bull at 25% requires B200 benchmarks beating by more than 30%, a multi-billion sovereign order, and an AMD follow-up delayed two quarters, giving EPS of 35.00 and 1400. The bear takes EPS to 25.00 at 30x for 750, and the Taiwan mechanism is brutal, roughly 90% of high-end GPU manufacturing halted and revenue down 60-70% for years. Because the base dominates, the rating is hold or accumulate weakness, entering 880-900 near the 50-day with a weekly close below the 100-day at 750 as the stop. I owe two admissions: confirmation bias from a one-sided narrative, and the fair counter that the price already embeds the bull with no margin of safety. Watch gross margin compression, sequential Data Center growth under 20%, and hyperscaler statements on internal silicon.

CrowdStrike near 340 is a quality-versus-price problem, and I think quality still wins over three to six months, so I want to be constructive but staged. Base case at 60%: Falcon keeps taking a disproportionate share of security budgets, ARR grows 30-35%, net retention stays above 120%, FCF margin holds above 30%, and while roughly 22x sales is rich, a PEG near 1.8 makes it defensible. At about 25x forward sales, in line with its historical premium, I get 385 in six months, supported technically by consolidation above a 50-day EMA that sits well above the 200-day, RSI 55-65, and OBV grinding higher. The bull at 25% needs a threat-environment shock, mid-cycle budget increases, Charlotte AI demand, or SentinelOne stumbling on execution; a 5% ARR guidance surprise triggers it and historically each 100bps of ARR outperformance adds roughly 10 dollars via multiple expansion, so a break of the 365 high on double volume points to 450 at 30x. The bear at 15% is macro plus the SBC question, with a 200bps rise in the ten-year de-rating the sector and net retention slipping under 115%, taking it to 270 at 17x once 320 and then 300 fail. The probability-weighted target is roughly 388 against 340, so I start with 60% of the position now, add the rest above 365, and stop out on a daily close below 315. My vulnerability is dependence on a sustained growth premium and market tolerance for stock comp. If wrong, check sequential billings growth, PANW and ZS commentary on sales cycles, and a VIX spike above 20. Failure to make new highs in one to two months would support the distribution read, about 30% likely.

Framing Micron over six to nine months, I want the recommendation conditional rather than absolute, because the setup is constructive but the entry matters more than the thesis. Base case at 60%: a steady recovery through 2024 into 2025 with HBM for AI servers as the tailwind, partially offset by cautious enterprise budgets and a slow consumer refresh, DRAM and NAND prices grinding higher and gross margin reaching roughly 45% by mid-2025 on about 55% revenue growth driven by price normalization rather than volume. At 18x forward on projected EPS of 7.78 that is 140. The chart cooperates: a bullish flag above the 50-day EMA near 128, RSI above 50 without stretching, OBV trending up. The bull at 25% is 165 on faster AI demand, an accelerated PC and smartphone refresh and supply discipline, worth roughly 30% more EPS; the bear at 15% is 105 on renewed macro weakness and an inventory glut, cutting EPS 40%. Skewed that way, a conditional buy is right: accumulate on dips into 130-135, hard stop at 119 where the bullish structure breaks, 2-3% sizing scaling to 4% if bull triggers appear. The backtest gives me some comfort, since crossing the 200-day from below with gross margin inflecting has produced an average 45% twelve-month return in three of the last four cycles, though four observations is thin. Recency bias is the danger, letting the AI narrative override how violently this industry has turned before. If 128 fails I check DRAMeXchange weekly spot, Samsung and Hynix commentary on inventory and pricing, and equipment lead times as a supply proxy. Two straight quarters of rising inventory days despite firm pricing would be the real red flag.

Eli Lilly over nine to twelve months is entirely a GLP-1 penetration question, and my confidence splits sharply: 85% on the growth thesis because the clinical data and uptake are not debatable, but only 55% on valuation, because the price already assumes near-perfect execution. Base case at 55%: manufacturing scales to meet demand, scripts compound 15-20% sequentially, no serious stockouts, share holds against Wegovy and Ozempic, FY2025 revenue reaches 65 billion with the GLP-1 franchise more than 45% of it. A DCF at 15% five-year revenue CAGR and 3% terminal growth, cross-checked at 64x forward against roughly 35% EPS growth for a PEG near 1.8, gives 980, with the stock likely basing in 850-900 on the 50-day EMA first. The bull at 30% and 1150 on 75x needs faster Zepbound uptake, a Novo stumble, or positive orforglipron data. The bear at 15% and 750 on 49x is safety signals or reimbursement resistance, with estimates cut 20% and about 500bps of margin damage from pricing pressure. The concentration risk is the honest vulnerability: one drug class carries the entire story. I should also consider that part of the recent move is flight-to-quality rather than fundamentals, which means a risk-on rotation into higher beta could hurt LLY even with clean results. My earliest falsifier is NBRX growth for Zepbound decelerating below 10% sequentially in Symphony or IQVIA data, then CagriSema, MariTide and VK2735 readouts, PBM formulary language from Express Scripts and CVS Caremark on 2026, and any surge in executive selling.

This request is retrospective rather than predictive, so my job is to assemble the March 2020 record accurately and then draw the structural lessons, not to forecast a ticker. The spine is the speed: the S&P 500 down 34% between February 19 and March 23, the fastest bear market entry on record, with Europe worse, the FTSE 100 off 36%, the DAX 39% and the CAC 40 42%, and VIX at 82.69 on March 16, a level unseen since 2008. Asia was not spared, Nikkei minus 23%, Hang Seng minus 21%, Sensex minus 38%. The sector story is the real analytical content, because it was a digital versus physical split rather than a normal cyclical rotation. Energy fell 37% with oil eventually printing negative 37 dollars a barrel on April 20 after travel restrictions erased about 30% of demand overnight; airlines and cruise lines lost 70-80%, AAL 73%, UAL 70%, CCL 58%. Against that, Zoom gained 396%, Moderna 434%, Netflix 67%, Microsoft 40%. Financials fell 32% sector-wide on credit provisions and zero rates, with Wells Fargo the worst at minus 37%. Geographically containment quality drove dispersion, Shanghai down only 3.4% and KOSPI 3.9% for 2020, while emerging markets suffered 100 billion of portfolio outflows, the largest month ever. The US recovered fastest on 2.2 trillion of CARES Act stimulus plus zero rates. Correlations going to near one during the panic then normalizing is worth stating, because it explains why diversification failed exactly when needed. For recovery shapes I want V for tech, U for services at eighteen to twenty-four months, L for legacy energy, and W as the second-wave risk.

For the Russia-Ukraine analysis the organizing insight is that this was a commodity and geopolitical shock transmitted into equities, not an equity shock, so I should lead with the commodity moves and let sector performance follow from them. Brent going from 90 to 139 dollars, up 60% in March 2022, and European gas up 300% because Russia supplied 40% of EU needs, is the causal engine; wheat up 50% and corn up 30% follows from Russia and Ukraine holding a combined 30% of global wheat exports. Equities were comparatively contained, the S&P 500 down 12% from its January peak to the March trough versus STOXX 600 down 15% on regional exposure, while MOEX crashed 39% on invasion day, bounced 26%, then halted for nearly a month. Safe havens behaved as expected, gold at 2,070 and DXY to 109. The ruble's 50% collapse to 142.46 and its artificial rescue via capital controls and export conversion requirements deserves explicit framing as policy, not recovery. Sector dispersion maps cleanly onto the shock: energy the best at plus 45% in Q1 with XOM up 53% and CVX 40%, defense averaging 25% as NATO members committed to 2% of GDP, fertilizers exploding with CF up 45% and Mosaic 50%, Deere up 25% on food security, while airlines fell 25% with jet fuel up 70% and tech dropped 15% except cybersecurity, CRWD 25% and PANW 30%. Europe absorbed the damage, the euro to 0.95. I want to close on structural change, deglobalization and friend-shoring, energy security as national security, defense spending as baseline, plus tail risks I should name but not overweight: nuclear escalation, a total energy cutoff, cyber warfare, Article 5.

The 2022-2023 tightening cycle needs to be told as a duration story, because that single mechanism explains equities, bonds, currencies and style rotation at once. The peaks first: US CPI at 9.1% in June 2022, the highest since 1981, Eurozone 10.6% in October, UK 11.1% the same month, with core peaking later and services stuck at 6-7%, which is what made policymakers abandon the transitory framing. Energy led at plus 50-100% year over year, food 30-50%, US shelter around 8%. The Fed's response was the most aggressive since the early 1980s, 0.25% to 5.5% in eighteen months alongside 95 billion a month of quantitative tightening; the ECB went from minus 0.5% to 4.5% and needed the Transmission Protection Instrument to contain peripheral spreads; the Bank of England went 0.1% to 5.25% while handling the September 2022 gilt crisis driven by unfunded tax cuts and pension deleveraging. In equities the duration effect is unmistakable: the S&P 500 down 25% peak to trough, tech down 30%, Meta minus 64%, Netflix minus 51%, Amazon minus 50%, against energy up 65% and financials outperforming by about 15%, the widest growth-versus-value gap since 2000. EAFE fell 16% and emerging markets 22%. The ten-year going from 1.5% to 5.0% produced the worst bond year on record, which is the point I want to make hardest, since bonds failed as a hedge precisely because the shock was inflationary. TIPS five-year forward breakevens peaking near 3.0% shows credibility held. The regime conclusion is that positive real rates returned after more than a decade, which forces a full recalibration rather than a cyclical adjustment.

China's property unwind needs to be told as a policy-induced deleveraging that became a demand shock, because that ordering explains everything downstream. Evergrande is the anchor, defaulting on more than 300 billion of liabilities in late 2021, equity off 90% from its peak and dollar bonds at twenty cents, but the systemic point is the sector's five trillion of debt against roughly 25% of GDP, with Country Garden, Sunac and Shimao following. The Three Red Lines rules on debt to cash, assets and equity are what turned leverage into a liquidity squeeze rather than a slow deflation. Then confidence broke: new home sales down 35% in 2022 and closer to 50% in tier-2 and tier-3 cities, stalled projects across more than 100 cities and mortgage payment strikes touching 222 billion of loans. The macro follow-through is unambiguous, GDP decelerating from 8.1% in 2021 to 3.0% in 2022, manufacturing PMI under 50 for stretches, urban youth unemployment at a record 21.3% in June 2023 before publication was suspended, retail sales negative in several months and outright deflationary prints in 2023. For global spillovers I want commodities to carry the argument since they are the cleanest transmission: iron ore from 220 to 80 dollars a ton, a 65% collapse, with BHP down 25% and Rio Tinto 30%, copper off 25%, aluminum 20% and rebar 15%. Structurally, with total debt above 280% of GDP, an aging population and urbanization past its peak, this is not a cycle to buy but a model change from property investment toward consumption and technology, with property stabilization plausibly taking twelve to eighteen months and 5-6% growth contingent on it.

March 2023 is best understood as a duration and deposit-structure failure, not a credit failure, and I want that distinction front and center. SVB died in 48 hours across March 9-10 on a 42 billion deposit run, the second-largest US bank failure, after a 15 billion loss on available-for-sale securities forced an emergency raise; the underlying problem was a 120 billion securities book carrying rate duration and 95% of deposits above the 250,000 FDIC limit, concentrated in venture and startup clients who all move at once. Mobile banking and social media compressed a classic run into a single day. The policy answer was a systemic risk exception protecting all depositors plus the Bank Term Funding Program. Credit Suisse then delivered the second shock, a 3.2 billion UBS takeover that wrote 17 billion of AT1 bonds to zero while equity holders got consideration, inverting the capital hierarchy, supported by 100 billion from the SNB and a 9.6 billion government loss guarantee, with European bank stocks down 20%. Regionals absorbed the contagion: Signature closed March 12 with 110 billion of assets, First Republic failed in April despite a 30 billion deposit infusion with the stock down 95%, PacWest and Western Alliance off 75% and 55%. The lurking exposure is commercial real estate, with regionals holding 70% of the five trillion market. Roughly 500 billion moved from deposits into money market funds. The rotation logic follows directly, defensives and rate beneficiaries outperforming and insurance and asset managers separating from banks, with confidence rebuilding over six to twelve months and lending standards settling over twelve to eighteen.

The European energy crisis is a case where price data alone tells the story, so I want the magnitudes to do the arguing. Pre-crisis Europe imported 40% of its gas from Russia, Germany 55%, which is the vulnerability that got weaponized. Nord Stream 1 falling to 20% capacity by July 2022 and shutting in August, with Nord Stream 2 and its eleven billion investment cancelled, drove Dutch TTF from 20 euros per megawatt hour to 340, a 1,600% move, with daily swings above 50%. Because gas plants set the marginal price under merit order, that volatility passed straight into power, German electricity at 1,000 euros against a historical 50 and French power above 1,500, aggravated by the French nuclear fleet running near 50% availability. The industrial consequences are the real economic content: aluminum smelters shutting a quarter of European capacity, BASF closing ammonia plants, European ammonia output down 70% with CF and Yara halting operations, glass and ceramics relocating, and intermittent shutdowns rippling into BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen. The policy response, an 80% storage mandate by November 2022, 25 FSRU units and five German LNG terminals in twelve months versus none before, plus the 180 euro gas price cap and joint purchasing, is what prevented a worse outcome. For markets, the tradable themes are an energy security premium, companies able to move production out of Europe, defensives holding up through an industrial recession, and firms with natural dollar hedges beating pure European exposure. The honest timeline is three to five years to fully replace Russian supply, which makes competitiveness loss structural rather than temporary.

The 2022-2023 tech correction is really one mechanism, the discount rate, working through public markets first and then the private ecosystem with a lag, and I want to trace it in that order. Publicly the NASDAQ Composite fell 36% from the November 2021 peak to the October 2022 trough, QQQ down 32% for its worst year since 2008, with roughly 4.5 trillion of mega-cap value erased across Apple down 27%, Microsoft 29%, Alphabet 39%, Amazon 50%, Meta 64% and Tesla 65%. The speculative tail was worse, Peloton down 91% and Zoom 86%, and the cleanest single statistic is median SaaS EV/Revenue compressing from 20x to 6x, which is multiple compression rather than fundamental collapse. The private lag then shows up hard: VC funding falling from 70 billion in Q4 2021 to 15 billion in Q4 2022, down 78%, with rounds above 100 million down 85% as crossover investors withdrew, median pre-money valuations halving, unicorn creation down 80%, and down rounds rising from a 5% historical norm to 25% of Series B and later. Behavior adjusted accordingly, burn cut 40-60%, runway extended from eighteen to thirty months, acqui-hires up 40%, CEO turnover doubling, and more than 150,000 tech layoffs in 2022 led by Amazon at 18,000 and Meta at 11,000. IPO issuance falling 94% to 8 billion from 150 billion closed the exit. Venture debt contracted about 50% even before SVB, which matters for why the bank's failure hit so hard. The recovery hinge is Fed pivot expectations, with ChatGPT's November 2022 launch supplying the next investment thesis.

Turkey in 2018 is the textbook case of a currency crisis driven by policy credibility rather than by any external shock, and the sequencing matters. The lira went from 4.5 to 7.2 per dollar in weeks, roughly 40% in August alone and 35% for the year, triggered proximately by the Pastor Brunson dispute and doubled steel and aluminum tariffs but fundamentally by doubts about central bank independence. The pass-through was immediate, CPI hitting 25% by October with food up 31%, and the balance sheet exposure is what made it dangerous: 216 billion of corporate FX debt, about 28% of GDP, so every depreciation step damaged solvency directly. The central bank's move from 8% to 24% was the largest single-year hike in modern Turkish history, but it came late, which is precisely why the first attempts to defend the currency failed. Domestically the damage shows in a 15% fall in bank lending, NPLs doubling from 3% to 6%, capital adequacy from 17% to 14%, TRY deposits down 12% as savers dollarized, and international funding costs up 400-500bp. Turkish Airlines took 4.5 billion of FX losses while exporters gained, textiles up 12%, which is the standard split. Contagion is worth quantifying but not exaggerating: the rand off 20%, the Argentine peso 50%, the real 15%, 15 billion of EM equity outflows in August and EM sovereign CDS wider by 100-150bp, plus BBVA down 8% and UniCredit 12% on subsidiary exposure. Stabilization near 5.5-6.0 by December came at the price of a 3% GDP contraction in 2019, with the current account improving from minus 5.6% to minus 1.8%.

Brexit is unusual among market shocks because the repricing happened in the currency rather than in equities, and the analysis is wrong if it does not lead with that. Sterling fell from 1.50 to 1.33 overnight, about 11%, then to 1.20 by October 2016, roughly 20% below pre-referendum. That devaluation is exactly why the FTSE 100 dropped only 8% and recovered within weeks, since its earnings are largely foreign currency, while the domestically exposed FTSE 250 fell 14% and stayed weak. That bifurcation is the single most useful observation in the whole episode. Gilts rallied hard, ten-year yields from 1.4% to 0.5% with the Bank cutting to 0.25%, and UK banks took the domestic hit, RBS down 38%, Barclays 32%, Lloyds 26%, while Europe caught contagion with the MIB off 12%. Through the Article 50 years the currency became a political instrument, volatility roughly three times normal, 2-3% daily moves routine, 3% down on the May deal rejection and a 12% rally from 1.21 to 1.35 on the December 2019 Conservative majority, then 1.37 on the trade deal. For financial services I want the relocation quantified rather than described: 5,500 firms losing passporting, about one trillion euros of assets moving to Dublin, Amsterdam, Paris and Frankfurt, 7,600 jobs relocated with Amsterdam gaining 2,800, and euro bond trading share shifting from 90% in London to 50% in Amsterdam. The real economy damage is slower and clearer in investment, down 25% from 2016 to 2020, productivity at 0.3% against an EU average of 2.1%, FDI halved, with sterling staying 10-15% below pre-referendum levels throughout.

H1N1 is valuable precisely as the counterexample to 2020, and the analytical spine should be that severity, not novelty, determines market impact. The WHO pandemic declaration in June 2009 produced only a 3% dip in global equities, and the reason sits in the case fatality rate of 0.02% against the 2-3% initially feared, even though 60.8 million Americans were infected with 274,000 hospitalizations and 12,469 deaths through April 2010. Total global economic cost of 45-55 billion is trivial next to 2020, though highly concentrated: Mexico alone lost 5.1 billion in tourism, the peso fell 15%, Mexico-US trade dropped 12% in Q2 2009 and remittances fell 15%. The sector responses are the tradable content. Vaccine makers gained on roughly 7 billion of contracts, Novartis up 18%, Sanofi 15%, GSK 12%, while Roche's Tamiflu revenue rose 435% to 3.2 billion with 1.2 billion of royalties to Gilead, and speculative preparedness names ran hardest, Chimerix up 156% and BioCryst 89%, which is the usual pattern of small caps overshooting on stockpiling headlines. On the other side, global passenger traffic fell 4.6% with Mexico routes down 40%, American Airlines losing 474 million, Mexican hotel occupancy halving versus a 10% US decline, Marriott revenue off 7.4% and Hilton 8.2%. Cruise lines fell 15% and recovered fast, which is the clearest evidence markets correctly repriced once severity was known. First vaccines in September 2009 and three billion doses by 2010 set the eighteen-month expectation that later became the baseline.

The Korean MERS episode is a study in how fear scales independently of case counts, and I want that paradox to organize the analysis. Only 186 confirmed cases and 38 deaths, though a 20.4% fatality rate explains the alarm, with 82% of transmission traced to healthcare facilities including Samsung Medical Center, yet the economic response was enormous: more than 16,000 quarantined and 2,900 schools closed affecting 1.6 million students. Tourism absorbed the damage, foreign arrivals down 45% year over year in June 2015 with Chinese visitors down 68%, annual tourism revenue off 2.6 billion, and the China-Korea corridor worth 7 billion falling 70% at the peak. That flows straight into duty free, Lotte down 40% and Shilla 35%, and into hotels, Seoul occupancy from 75% to 45% with rates off 25%, plus Korean Air down 8% and Asiana 12%. Domestic consumption reacted to crowd avoidance rather than illness, foot traffic at Lotte Shopping and Shinsegae down 30%, food service down 25%, cinema attendance down 40% and theme parks down 60%, while online shopping rose 35% and masks rose 1,000%. That substitution pattern, not the epidemiology, is the durable lesson. The correlation work is worth stating, won weakness at minus 0.8 against tourism arrivals, tech showing little sensitivity, and housing essentially unaffected because the shock was short. Recovery was quick where behavior drove it, consumer spending back within six months and volatility normal by September 2015, but slower where reputation drove it, tourism twelve months and medical tourism eighteen.

Zika is the case where the market impact ran through fertility risk and event risk rather than mortality, so the framework has to be different from a normal outbreak analysis. Brazil reported 1.5 million suspected cases spreading to more than 60 countries, WHO declared an emergency in February 2016, and the reason it mattered was more than 4,000 microcephaly cases, which targeted a specific demographic, pregnant travelers, rather than the general population. The World Bank's 3.5 billion regional cost estimate is small, so I should be careful to separate Zika's effect from Brazil's concurrent recession and political crisis. The cleanest attribution is the roughly 400bp of Bovespa underperformance, minus 13% against MSCI LatAm at minus 9%, plus tourism revenue down 10.2% or 2.8 billion and the real down 17%. The Olympics gave the story a datable event: more than 150 athletes questioning participation including the top four golfers, Rio hotel bookings down 30% and international packages down 45%, and travel insurance claims up 200% with insurers adding Zika exclusions. On the beneficiary side the pattern is familiar and speculative, NIH allocating 1.1 billion with more than 45 vaccine candidates, Inovio up 180% and GeoVax 145%, while the durable revenue actually accrued to diagnostics, Abbott and Roche seeing 40-60% growth, and vector control like Oxitec's 15 million in contracts. The structural tail I want to note is the 15% fertility decline in the worst-affected countries, and that tourism took eighteen to twenty-four months to recover with performance inversely tracking mosquito season.

The 2017 North Korea episode is the best modern illustration that geopolitical risk gets absorbed by fundamentals when the tail never materializes, and the numbers make that argument for me. Twenty-three missile tests, ICBM launches in July and November and a sixth nuclear test in September, yet the KOSPI finished 2017 up 21.8% with the won 13% stronger against the dollar. That is the central paradox of the analysis: the market closest to the risk performed best. Individual events did move things, the fire and fury remark knocking the KOSPI down 2.1% in a day and lifting VIX from 10.9 to 16.1, and safe havens behaved textbook, gold reaching 1,357 during the September test, the yen from 114 to 108, ten-year Treasury yields falling from 2.6% to 2.0%, the franc up 3% against the euro, and even bitcoin up 20% with Korean demand notable. Regionally the Nikkei rose 19.1% but lagged at peak tension, Shanghai gained only 6.6%, while the Hang Seng at plus 36% benefited from mainland liquidity and distance. Defense was the persistent trade, Northrop up 35%, Lockheed 32%, Raytheon 25%, Hanwha Systems 25% and Korea Aerospace 18%, with roughly 15 billion of Aegis-related regional deployment. The correlation detail I find most telling is Korean equities showing minus 0.3 correlation with US markets during tensions versus a normal plus 0.7, and foreign investor won hedge ratios rising from 60% to 85%. Successive tests produced diminishing reactions, and the PyeongChang diplomatic window closed the year calmly.

Balakot in February 2019 is worth analyzing because two nuclear-armed states escalated and the market reaction was still measured, which tells you something about how risk premia get priced when de-escalation is expected. The chain runs from the Pulwama bombing on February 14 killing 40 personnel, to Indian air strikes on February 26, the first cross-border air action since 1971, to the February 27 dogfight and pilot capture, then release on March 1. Indian markets took it calmly in absolute terms, the Sensex off 2.6% in the crisis week with midcaps worse at minus 4.1%, the rupee from 71.0 to 73.2 or 3.1%, ten-year yields up 25bp to 7.8%, and India VIX from 16.5 to 24.3, a 47% jump that captures the fear better than the index decline does. The asymmetry is the analytical point: Pakistan's KSE-100 fell 8.4%, its worst week in eighteen months, the rupee slid from 139 to 142 into an existing balance of payments crisis, reserves fell 400 million, and sovereign CDS widened 150bp to 950bp, which is distress pricing, with HBL down 15% and MCB 12%. Sectorally the pattern is textbook, Hindustan Aeronautics up 22% and Bharat Electronics 18% against IndiGo down 12% and SpiceJet 18%. Contagion was modest, Shanghai off 0.8%, Thailand 2.1%, FTSE 1.2%, S&P futures 0.8% in Asian hours, with gold up 1.8% and the franc 1.2%. The recovery speed is the conclusion I want: Indian equities recouped losses within ten trading days and both currencies normalized inside three weeks, so the durable effect is higher structural defense spending, not repricing.

Nagorno-Karabakh in 2020 is a case where the interesting market content is not equity drawdowns, which barely happened, but infrastructure risk and the defense technology read-through. The 44-day war from September 27, the largest escalation since the 1994 ceasefire, produced more than 6,000 casualties, Azerbaijan retaking over 300 settlements and seven districts, and a November 9 ceasefire with 2,000 Russian peacekeepers on a five-year mandate. The energy question is whether pipelines were actually at risk: BTC carries 600,000 barrels a day over 1,768 kilometers and the Southern Gas Corridor moves 10 bcm a year to Europe, and the market answer was a modest 3 to 5 dollar premium on oil while Azerbaijani output held at 760,000 bpd and 24 bcm. That resilience is itself the finding. Equity reactions split along alignment, Borsa Istanbul up 2.8% with Turkey backing Baku, MOEX essentially flat at minus 0.5% given Russia's balancing act, and TEDPIX down 3.2% on refugee and border pressure, while Georgia's 2.5 billion transit economy sat exposed. The most consequential thread is military technology: Baykar drones proving decisive drove roughly 5 billion in new orders, Israeli Harop and Spike systems contributed, and the lessons redirected global procurement worth more than 100 billion, with EU defense thinking shifting toward drone warfare. Commodity exposure runs through Armenia's Zangezur copper at 150,000 tonnes. Post-conflict, political risk premiums rose 200-300bp regionally, pipeline insurance costs by 50 million a year, and the Middle Corridor gained strategic weight alongside 50 billion of reconstruction need.

The Soleimani episode is the cleanest example I have of a geopolitical shock that markets priced and unpriced within a week, and the analysis should be honest that the initial fear was larger than the eventual impact. The January 3 strike and the January 8 Iranian missile response on US bases in Iraq were the first direct Iranian attack on US forces, so the tail risk was genuine, yet Brent moved only from 68 to 71, up 4.4% with a 72.50 intraday high, and WTI 4.6% to 63.84. Twenty percent of global oil transits Hormuz, so the restraint in that move is notable, and energy equities tracked it, ConocoPhillips up 4.2%, Exxon 3.1%, Chevron 2.8%. Equity declines were shallow: the S&P down 0.7%, the Dow 162 points, STOXX 600 off 1.2% with the DAX 1.7%, the Nikkei 1.9%, MSCI EM 1.5%, and Hang Seng actually up 0.3%. Regional markets were more sensitive but still contained, Tadawul minus 1.8% recovering in 48 hours, Dubai and Abu Dhabi minus 2.1%, Tel Aviv minus 2.6%, Borsa Istanbul minus 3.4% on proximity, and Beirut minus 4.2% compounding an existing crisis. The safe haven flows behaved exactly as theory predicts, gold up 1.8% to 1,588, ten-year yields from 1.88% to 1.78%, the yen from 108.6 to 107.8, the franc up 0.8%. Markets recovered about 70% of losses within a week, crude was back to pre-crisis inside ten days, and VIX fell from 18.5 to 13.2, so my conclusion is that mutual restraint plus strong underlying fundamentals dissolved the war premium quickly.

Deutsche Bank across 2016 to 2019 is a slow-burn solvency-perception crisis rather than a sudden run, and the analysis needs to explain why it never became systemic despite the headline exposure. The trigger was the September 2016 DOJ demand for 14 billion dollars over mortgage securities, which knocked the stock 8.5% in a day, but the underlying trend was worse: shares from 28 euros in 2015 to 7.20 by 2019, a 74% decline and the worst among global systemically important banks, market cap from 33 billion to 15 billion, below tangible book, and five-year CDS widening from 150bp to 450bp, which is the counterparty market pricing real doubt. The number everyone quoted was the 41 trillion euro notional derivative book, roughly sixteen times German GDP, and the honest framing is that notional overstates risk once netting and collateral are applied, though the scrutiny it drew was itself damaging. The self-reinforcing mechanism is what matters: investment banking revenue falling 15% a year as clients de-risked, more than 50 billion of prime brokerage assets withdrawn, 5 billion of added funding cost from margin, and accelerated migration to central clearing. Contagion was sector-wide, SX7P down 35% and lagging the market by 25 points, UniCredit minus 45%, SocGen minus 28%, with Brexit compounding RBS at minus 42%. Regulation forced the fix, a failed 2016 stress test at minus 7.8% CET1 adverse, 8 billion raised, 15 billion of TLAC instruments. By 2019 ROE moved from minus 2.8% to plus 0.5%, CET1 from 11.8% to 13.6%, notional cut to 25 trillion.

Italy in 2016-2017 is the doom loop in its purest form, and I want the causality stated in both directions rather than treating the banks and the sovereign as separate problems. The stock of bad debt is the starting point, 360 billion euros of NPLs at 18% of total loans, three times the European average, against which Italian banks also held 385 billion of domestic government bonds. That is the loop: sovereign stress impairs bank capital, bank rescues raise sovereign risk, and the 90%-plus correlation between bank equities and BTP prices is the measurable proof. Monte dei Paschi is the emblem, a 5.4 billion shortfall becoming a 20 billion government package, the largest European rescue since 2008, with the state taking 68% after private capital failed, 28 billion of NPLs moved to a state vehicle at 21 cents on the euro, 1,200 branches closed and 8,000 jobs cut, after the ECB assessment found a 14.6 billion gap. The wider damage is severe, 150 billion or 60% of Italian bank market value gone, the banking index down 65% peak to trough, UniCredit off 75% needing 13 billion, Intesa the relative winner at minus 35%, and Veneto Banca and Popolare di Vicenza liquidated at 17 billion of taxpayer cost, with CDS at 400-600bp. On the sovereign side BTP yields moved from 1.5% to 2.8% with the spread to Bunds at 250bp and Moody's cutting to Baa2. The resolution came from QE buying more than 350 billion of BTPs plus supervisory capital add-ons, and by 2019 NPLs were down to 200 billion, CET1 from 11.5% to 14.2%, ROE from minus 2.5% to plus 4.5%.
